newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Manmohan Singh says economy faltering.
newsitem.headline: India's Manmohan Singh says economy faltering.

text.p: Former finance minister Manmohan Singh said India's economic reforms were faltering because of a lack of clarity in the government's policies but said he never wanted his old job back again.
Singh was quoted by Outlook magazine on Thursday as calling for steps to bring the country's fiscal deficit to four percent from the current 5.8 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
Analysts say the ratio could come down to between 5.1 and 5.4 percent in the current (1996/97) year.
Singh's interview was published a day before Finance Minister P. Chidambaram is scheduled to unveil the federal budget for the 1997/98 fiscal year starting April 1.

"It is an indifferent performance," the architect of India's sweeping economic reforms from 1991 to 1996 said of the nine-month-old government of Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda which Singh's Congress party supports reluctantly.

"It has not been able to cash in on the opportunity to lift the economy further after the Congress government had successfully turned it around," Singh said. "Frankly the government is acting as if it's an election year."

This week the government unveiled a populist measure that will add $2.2 billion in food subsidies for the poor. A commission recently recommended raising annual payouts to civil servants by $2.4 billion.
Chidambaram has to walk a tightrope between communists and liberals who often seem strange bedfellows in the fractious 15-party government.
Most politicians say Deve Gowda could call mid-term elections if he feels threatened by Congress's growing criticism of his government.

"They should take steps to bring the fiscal deficit down to four percent," Singh said. "They should carry out overall macro-economic reforms and complete the process of tax refroms which the country needs badly."
"The aim should be to create a macro-economic environment conducive enough for a GDP growth rate of at least seven percent," Singh said.
He did not say what steps the government ought to take.

The Congress suffered its worst-ever defeat in general elections last year and was then forced to support Deve Gowda's 13-party centre-left coalition to ward off a challenge from the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party.
Singh said the rout had nothing to do with his policies.
"The Congress stands by its earlier policy which reformed the country's economy. But for that policy the country's economy would have gone to pieces," he said.
When Singh took charge, India's growth rate had slumped to 3.5 percent, inflation was hovering around 17 percent and exports were languishing.

"When we left, export growth was high at 20 percent in dollar terms, inflation was low at below four percent, foreign exchange reserves exceeded $20 billion and India's credit-rating was higher than ever," he said.

Asked if he would want to become the finance minister again, Singh said: "No, never. I do not want to go back to the same seat again. I have spent enough time as finance minister and done what I could have done for the country."
